nameStory: Scopoli's Shearwater gets its name from Giovanni Antonio Scopoli, an 18th-century Italian naturalist who studied Mediterranean wildlife. The 'shearwater' part comes from these birds' amazing ability to fly just inches above the ocean surface, literally shearing through the water with their wingtips as they glide effortlessly over the waves.
description: Scopoli's Shearwater is a graceful seabird that spends most of its life soaring over ocean waters. These medium-sized birds have a distinctive two-toned appearance - brownish-gray on top and clean white underneath. They're built for life at sea, with long, narrow wings perfect for gliding over waves without much flapping. In New England waters, they're quite rare visitors, usually spotted far offshore during their ocean wanderings.

idTips.label: Two-toned coloring
idTips.description: Clean white underparts contrast sharply with brownish-gray upperparts and darker wing feathers, creating a striking two-toned appearance when seen from below or side

idTips.label: Pale yellow bill
idTips.description: Bill is pale yellow with a distinctive dark patch near the tip, giving it a two-toned appearance that's visible even at distance through binoculars

idTips.label: Gliding flight style
idTips.description: Flies with stiff, straight wings held horizontally, gliding low over waves with minimal flapping - you'll hear the whoosh of air over wings rather than wingbeats

idTips.label: Darker wing edges
idTips.description: Wing feathers are noticeably darker than the brownish-gray back, creating a contrasting pattern most visible when the bird banks or turns

idTips.label: Ocean behavior
idTips.description: Skims incredibly close to wave surfaces, often disappearing briefly behind swells before reappearing, rarely coming close to shore

habitat: In New England waters, Scopoli's Shearwaters are found exclusively far offshore in deep ocean waters, typically many miles from the coast. They prefer areas where ocean currents create upwelling that brings fish and small marine creatures to the surface. You'll need to take a whale watching boat or deep-sea fishing charter to have any chance of spotting one.

seasonality.spring: Rare visitors may appear in late spring as they begin their Atlantic wanderings after Mediterranean breeding season ends.
seasonality.summer: Most likely season to spot these rare visitors in New England waters, though still extremely uncommon even on offshore trips.
seasonality.fall: Occasionally seen during fall migration periods as birds move through Atlantic waters, but sightings remain very rare.
seasonality.winter: Extremely rare in winter months as most birds remain in warmer Atlantic waters far from New England.

funFact: Scopoli's Shearwaters can lock their wings in place using special tendons, allowing them to glide for hours without a single wingbeat - they're essentially living gliders that can sleep while soaring over the ocean!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Cory's Shearwater, which is much more common in New England waters. Scopoli's tends to have a slightly more contrasting dark wingtip pattern and the bill's dark tip patch is usually more distinct, but definitive identification often requires expert knowledge and good viewing conditions.
contextualKnowledge: Until recently, Scopoli's Shearwater was considered the same species as Cory's Shearwater, so older field guides and bird lists may not distinguish between them. Many birders still group them together when reporting sightings due to the difficulty of telling them apart in the field.
compareHints: Compared to its close relative Cory's Shearwater, Scopoli's typically shows more contrasting dark wing edges and a more distinct dark patch on the bill tip. However, these differences can be subtle and variable, making field identification challenging even for experienced birders. Cory's Shearwater is also much more common in New England waters, so any large shearwater you see is statistically more likely to be a Cory's.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Cory's Shearwater is much larger and paler than its closest relative, Scopoli's Shearwater, which is found in the Mediterranean.
